mutants.rationale: The interleaved order (re_1, im_1, re_2, ...) is a different convention: R in that order is P (x) I2 + Q (x) J1, does not commute with the block J_2, and equals the block R only for 1 x 1 matrices.
R(A*) uses the conjugate transpose (P^T, -Q^T); a plain transpose (P^T, Q^T) gives R(A^T), which differs from R(A*) whenever Q != 0.
The Hermitian matrix [[1,2],[2,1]] has determinant -3 and is indefinite; asserting that it or its realification is positive semidefinite contradicts the exact minors / elimination.
For A = 1 + i read Tr R(A) = 2 as twice the complex trace 1 + i; it is twice the REAL part only.
Use [[P,Q],[-Q,P]] (imaginary part first / J replaced by -J): still multiplicative, but it is R of the conjugate and R(AB) differs.
diag(1,0,0,0) is a positive trace-one real matrix but does not commute with J_2, hence is no R(A).
diag(1,-1) implements complex conjugation: it anticommutes with J, so it is not R of a complex matrix.
For a 2 x 4 doubled operator the test is J_1 M = M J_2 between different carriers; the square-only "commutes with J" is the wrong test.
The integer matrix [[1,-1],[2,-1]] squares to -I but is neither J nor commutes with J: J is declared, not forced by J^2 = -I.
Only +-J commute with J, but J^2 = -I has 26 integer solutions in the box [-5,5]; reading J as unique hides the declaration.
Symmetry alone does not put a real matrix in the image: diag(1,2,3,4) is symmetric but does not commute with J_2.
A complex structure needs even real dimension; a 3 x 3 real matrix has no J_n to commute with.
